co_bucksnort_slab.blurb: A broad granite slab above Elk Creek Road in the South Platte hills near Pine, mostly climbed on gear with a handful of bolted lines and a couple of top ropes. The style is classic South Platte friction: thin cracks, small nubs and edges, with a lot of 5.10 to 5.12 slab climbing beyond the easier lines. Classic Dihedral (5.7+, trad) is the moderate standout, while Slippery When Wet and Slippery When Dry give the harder crowd something to chew on. Friction is best in the cooler hours, and the slab lives up to its names when damp. A few older bolts are thin quarter-inchers, so judge them with care. Most climbs can be finished by walking off or rappelling.
co_bucksnort_slab.parking_note: The slab sits right beside Elk Creek Road, about 2 miles east of the town of Pine. Roadside space is tight, so expect to leave the car a short way along and walk back.
co_bucksnort_slab.approach: A short walk from the road to the base; the wall rises straight up on the north side.

co_bitty_buttress.blurb: A small granite crag on the north side of Boulder Canyon, split into several short sections: a main buttress, a peapod-shaped feature, an amphitheater and some side gullies. The rock is featured and speckled with lichen, and the mix runs from moderate multi-pitch trad to bolted lines up into the 5.12s and beyond. Bitty Buttress (5.8+, trad, 3p) is the namesake moderate, with The Buzz and Rise and Shine for the sport crowd and The Lorax at the top of the scale. The walk in is longer than for the neighboring Blob Rock, so plan on a bit of a hike. Descend by walking off the back to the northwest and down a gully. A large loose block sits near the top of the namesake route, so take care near the finish.
co_bitty_buttress.parking_note: Use the roadside pullout on the north side of the canyon, just west of the pullout used for Cob Rock, about 6.6 miles up from the bridge at the canyon mouth.

co_haus_rock.blurb: A compact granite outcrop on the south flank of Porcupine Peak above Keystone, around 9,800 feet, and one of the best-known sport crags in Summit County. Nearly everything is bolted, and many lines can be run as top ropes. The shaded north side holds the moderate slabs, the west side has a few mid-grade lines, and the steeper south side is where the 5.12 and 5.13 routes live, including Crystal Ball, Sky Pilot and Macho Picasso. Its altitude and shady aspects make it a pleasant escape when the lowlands are hot, and summer weekends bring crowds. Wear shoes with grip for the talus on the way up.
co_haus_rock.parking_note: Park in the dirt pullout on the north side of the road to Montezuma, a short way past the Keystone Powerline lot, roughly a mile and a half east of the town. It holds only a handful of cars and is shared with nearby crags.
co_haus_rock.approach: Take the steep trail up the embankment and climb over talus and a small rockslide to reach the south side of the rock; the moderate north side is reached by a cairned path.

co_mountain_rose.blurb: A small pair of granite crags on the south side of Boulder Canyon, above the river near Castle Rock along an old aqueduct roadbed. Much of the rock was blasted away when the aqueduct went in, so quality swings from solid to crumbly; pick lines with care. The climbing is mostly short bolted face climbing in the 5.9 to 5.11 range, plus a few trad lines, with Sick Puppy (5.12b, sport) the hardest of the classic bolted routes. Climbs are roughly 50 to 80 feet on the larger crag and shorter on the smaller one. It makes an easy-going warm-up spot and offers an open, high feel with views across to Castle Rock.
co_mountain_rose.approach: Cross the footbridge by Castle Rock, walk along the base of Broken Rock (a short slab scramble may be needed at high water), then angle uphill to the aqueduct roadbed and follow it southwest a couple hundred paces to the larger crag.

co_paleosol_wall.blurb: A south-facing basalt buttress about 50 feet tall on the rim of Grand Mesa, near 10,000 feet. The dark rock is high quality and ranges from blank patches to heavily pocketed faces, and the wall offers bolted lines alongside crack and roof climbs on gear. Most routes sit between 5.8 and 5.11, with the bulk around 5.10. Ft Mac Gravy Train, Flat Rock Flight and Paleoflow are the trad favorites, while Ultramafic, Punctuated Equilibrium, Jungle Gym and Mass Wasting are the sport ones. Routes are reached from the top, scrambling down beside boulders to cairned anchors; the walk out is east around a loose gully and up a short class 3 step to the rim. The high elevation keeps it cool in summer.
co_paleosol_wall.parking_note: From the fork at the top of Land's End Road, continue about 1.9 miles south and leave the car at the roadside near a lone bushy pine standing at the cliff edge.
co_paleosol_wall.approach: From the lone pine, scramble down beside a couple of big boulders to the cairns that mark the anchors above the wall.

ct_chatfield_hollow_main_wall.blurb: A compact gneiss cliff in a hardwood forest above Route 80 in Killingworth, inside Chatfield Hollow State Park. The grey, gritty rock offers overhanging walls, roofs, aretes, cracks and slabs, and holds range from finger cracks and jugs to slopers, edges and pockets. It is mainly a trad crag, with some sport, top-rope and mixed lines, from easy moderates up through the 5.12s and a few 5.13s. Forearm Frenzy, Shape Shifter, The Cold Vein and Magic Central are among the standouts. Because the wall is so compact, you can pack a lot of routes into a day. The cliff top has thin, fragile soil, so stick to bare rock and established paths.
ct_chatfield_hollow_main_wall.parking_note: Use the rough pullout on the left of Route 80, a few tenths of a mile west of the entrance to Chatfield Hollow State Park.
ct_chatfield_hollow_main_wall.approach: Walk uphill along the road for about 150 yards, then enter the woods just before the guardrail; a faint path leads to the base under 100 yards away, while a right fork reaches the top.

ct_bear_rock.blurb: A single bolted cliff about 70 feet tall in the woods of Durham, near the Mattabesett Trail in Cockaponsett State Forest. The rock is a sharp gneiss-quartz mix, and the sport lines are mostly juggy overhangs on one face, with well-placed bolts and lower-offs on top. Grades run from the high 5.7s up to 5.13a, though most routes fall in the 5.11 to 5.12 range, with a small set of boulder problems nearby. The Revenant, The Color of Aluminum and Chubby Chaser are among the better-known lines, and Posie's Porpoise gives a 5.10b. The wall is slow to dry after rain. Leading is easier here than top-roping, thanks to the overhangs.
ct_bear_rock.parking_note: From Higganum Road, follow Harvey Road about 0.4 miles to a small unmarked pullout on the right, off the blue-blazed trail. The lot is tiny, so share rides if you can.
ct_bear_rock.approach: Follow the blue-blazed trail north of the road for roughly half a mile, cross a swampy stream and take the right fork; the cliff is on your left.

ct_bear_rock_climbs.blurb: The bolted lines on the main face at Bear Rock in Durham, mostly steep and juggy sport climbing in the woods near the Mattabesett Trail. Most routes fall between 5.11 and 5.12, with a few easier lines in the 5.7 to 5.10 range and The Revenant (5.13a) at the top. The Color of Aluminum, Chubby Chaser, Natural Born Salmon Killer, Salmon Chasers and Sh*t Ticket (5.11b) are all worth a look, and Posie's Porpoise (5.10b) is a good place to warm up. Anchors are bolted, and leading tends to be easier than top-roping because of the overhanging profile. Bring a few friends and share a car, since the trailhead is tiny.

ct_historical_routes.blurb: The older, mostly gear-protected lines on the Firewall, a basalt traprock cliff on the Metacomet Ridge in Southington, just north of Ragged Mountain. These routes date to the early days of climbing here and are mainly traditional leads and top-rope lines, with the bulk falling between 5.9 and 5.11 and a handful of easier ones. Some moderates are sparsely bolted or protected, so leaders should expect to place gear and keep their heads. Traprock tends to offer steep faces, cracks and corners, and the cliff is a short stroll from the lake. A good choice for climbers who like a traditional flavor without a long hike.
ct_historical_routes.parking_note: Take Ledge Road from Crooked Street and turn into the Crescent Lake lot about 1.6 miles along.
ct_historical_routes.approach: Walk the south shoreline trail from the lake lot for around 10 to 15 minutes until it bends north to an open slope of hemlocks, then climb a few hundred feet to the cliff.

ct_pootatuck_state_forest.blurb: A scattering of granitic gneiss boulders in the hills of New Fairfield, next to Squantz Pond State Park. Bouldering here is spread across several sectors set along the forest's fire road and trails, with the Fire Road and Red Trail groups holding the most problems. Grades run from the low end of the V scale to the high V8s and V9, with plenty in the V4 to V7 band, so there is something for most climbers, though some of the harder problems look very difficult. The area is quiet and woodsy, and some boulders have been cleaned. Bring pads and be ready to hike between groups.
ct_pootatuck_state_forest.parking_note: Use the small lots off Shortwoods Road or Pine Hill Road, or walk in through Squantz Pond State Park.
